item.content:encoded:
The Australian Embassy Direct Aid Program (DAP) 2026–27 is now open for applications, providing an opportunity for individuals, community groups and non-governmental organisations to seek support for small development projects in Lebanon and Syria.

Administered by the Australian Embassy, the Direct Aid Program is designed as a flexible small-grants mechanism that focuses on relieving humanitarian hardship and advancing developmental objectives. Projects supported through the program must be consistent with Australia’s international relations and public diplomacy objectives.

For organisations and community actors working to address humanitarian challenges, strengthen communities and contribute to development outcomes in Lebanon and Syria, the program can provide an avenue to seek financial support for practical, locally relevant initiatives.

The application deadline for the current funding round is 11 September 2026. Applications must be submitted through the SmartyGrants application platform.

What Is the Australian Embassy Direct Aid Program?

The Direct Aid Program (DAP) is a small-grants program operated by the Australian Embassy. Unlike programs that are designed primarily around individual educational or professional development, DAP focuses on supporting development projects and initiatives intended to address humanitarian hardship and developmental needs.

According to the Australian Embassy, the program is flexible and considers proposals for small development projects from eligible applicants involved in development activities on a not-for-profit basis.

The program therefore provides an opportunity for eligible applicants to present practical projects that have the potential to contribute to communities in Lebanon and Syria.

Applicants should ensure that their proposed initiatives fit within the program’s objectives and funding requirements before beginning the application process. The Embassy specifically advises prospective applicants to review the DAP guidelines before submitting an application.

Key Objectives of the Direct Aid Program

The Australian Embassy identifies two central areas of focus for DAP:

  1. Relieving humanitarian hardship
  2. Advancing developmental objectives

Projects should also be consistent with Australia’s international relations and public diplomacy objectives.

This means that prospective applicants should think carefully about the humanitarian or development problem their project is addressing and demonstrate how the proposed intervention can make a meaningful contribution.

A strong proposal should therefore clearly communicate:

  • The problem or need being addressed.
  • The community or beneficiaries who will benefit.
  • The proposed activities.
  • How the activities respond to the identified need.
  • The expected development or humanitarian outcomes.
  • Why the proposed intervention is appropriate for the local context.
  • How the project aligns with the objectives of the Direct Aid Program.

The source provided does not list specific project themes or detailed assessment criteria, so applicants should consult the official DAP Guidelines before preparing their proposals.

Who Can Apply for the Australian Embassy Direct Aid Program?

The program is open to several types of applicants.

According to the Australian Embassy, the DAP committee assesses proposals for small development projects submitted by:

  • Individuals
  • Community groups
  • Non-governmental organisations

Applicants must be engaged in development activities on a not-for-profit basis.

This makes the program potentially relevant to grassroots actors and organisations that are working directly on development or humanitarian challenges rather than exclusively to large international institutions.

Geographic Eligibility

The current Direct Aid Program described on the Australian Embassy’s Lebanon website focuses on projects in:

  • Lebanon
  • Syria

The source does not indicate that applicants from every country worldwide are eligible. Instead, the program is presented specifically in relation to humanitarian and development objectives in Lebanon and Syria.

The source also does not identify a particular race, ethnicity, continent, or age group as an eligibility requirement.

Why Is This Grant Opportunity Important?

Lebanon and Syria have experienced significant humanitarian and socioeconomic challenges, creating substantial needs for humanitarian assistance, protection, livelihoods and other forms of development support.

The Australian Embassy’s information highlights the scale of these challenges. It states that Lebanon has experienced an unprecedented financial and economic crisis and that millions of people living in the country require humanitarian assistance. The Embassy also notes the effects of poverty among Lebanese communities, displaced Syrian households and Palestine refugee populations.

Syria, meanwhile, has faced more than a decade of conflict, resulting in extensive humanitarian needs and large-scale displacement. The Embassy’s background information describes millions of people in Syria as requiring humanitarian assistance and notes the significant number of internally displaced people and Syrian refugees in neighbouring countries, including Lebanon.

Against this backdrop, small community-based development projects can play an important role in responding to specific needs at the local level.

What Types of Applicants May Find This Opportunity Relevant?

Because DAP is intended for small development projects, it may be particularly relevant to applicants already working within communities and seeking support to implement practical initiatives.

Potentially relevant applicants include:

Individuals involved in development activities

Individuals who are undertaking eligible development-oriented activities on a not-for-profit basis may consider whether their work fits the program’s requirements.

Community groups

Local community groups may use the opportunity to seek support for initiatives addressing identified humanitarian or developmental needs within their communities.

Non-governmental organisations

NGOs involved in development activities can also submit proposals, provided their activities and proposed project meet the relevant program requirements.

However, applicants should not assume that being an individual, community group or NGO automatically guarantees eligibility. The Embassy specifically directs applicants to review the DAP Guidelines and funding requirements before applying.

What Should Applicants Consider Before Applying?

Before starting the application, prospective applicants should first establish whether their proposed project fits within the program.

The Australian Embassy explicitly advises applicants to check the DAP guidelines before starting the application so that they understand the program and its funding requirements.

A useful preparation process is to:

  1. Read the official DAP Guidelines carefully.
    Understand the program’s objectives, eligibility requirements and funding conditions.
  2. Define the development or humanitarian problem.
    Clearly identify the need your project intends to address.
  3. Identify the beneficiaries.
    Explain who will benefit from the proposed project and why they need the intervention.
  4. Develop a practical project plan.
    Outline the activities that will be undertaken and how they will contribute to the intended outcomes.
  5. Ensure the proposal is not-for-profit.
    The program specifically refers to individuals, community groups and NGOs engaged in development activities on a not-for-profit basis.
  6. Consider alignment with DAP objectives.
    Make the connection between the proposed project, humanitarian hardship, developmental objectives and the broader objectives identified by the Australian Embassy.
  7. Prepare the application before the deadline.
    Avoid waiting until the final day to submit, particularly if supporting information or clarification is required.

How to Apply for the Australian Embassy Direct Aid Program

Applications for the current round are being accepted through SmartyGrants.

The Australian Embassy states that applicants have until 11 September 2026 to submit their applications through the designated application platform.

Application deadline: 11 September 2026

Applicants should use the official application process and consult the program guidelines before submitting their proposals.

Apply through SmartyGrants – Australian Embassy DAP 2026–27.

APPLY HERE

Important Program Guidelines

The DAP application should not be approached simply as a request for financial assistance. Applicants should first understand what the Australian Embassy is seeking to support.

The Embassy provides a dedicated DAP Guidelines document for applicants. The guidelines are intended to explain the program and its funding requirements.

Prospective applicants should therefore read the guidelines in full before preparing their final proposal.

Read the DAP Guidelines

Previous Projects Funded by the Australian Embassy

The Australian Embassy website also provides information about projects funded through previous DAP rounds.

Applicants can review examples from previous funding years, including:

  • 2024–2025
  • 2023–2024
  • 2022–2023
  • 2021–2022
  • 2020–2021
  • 2019–2020
  • 2018–2019
  • 2017–2018
  • Earlier funding periods dating back to 2013–2014 and previous years.

Reviewing previous projects can be useful for applicants seeking to understand the types of development initiatives that have previously received support. However, past funding should not be interpreted as a guarantee that a similar project will receive funding in the current round.

Australia’s Broader Humanitarian Engagement in Lebanon and Syria

The Direct Aid Program sits within a broader context of Australian humanitarian assistance in the region.

The Australian Embassy states that, since 2011, the Australian Government has provided more than AU$500 million in humanitarian assistance to support people in need in Lebanon, Syria and Jordan. It also states that more than AU$120 million had been provided to Lebanon since 2017.

According to the Embassy, this assistance in Lebanon has supported vulnerable Lebanese communities and Syrian refugees through areas including:

  • Humanitarian assistance
  • Protection services
  • Livelihood opportunities

The funding has been delivered through UN agencies, international and local humanitarian organisations and other partners.

This broader humanitarian engagement provides important context for understanding the role of the Direct Aid Program and its focus on humanitarian hardship and development.

Key Facts About the Australian Embassy Direct Aid Program 2026–27

Detail Information
Program Australian Embassy Direct Aid Program (DAP)
Funding round 2026–27
Category Grant
Focus Humanitarian hardship and development
Geographic focus Lebanon and Syria
Eligible applicant types Individuals, community groups and NGOs
Applicant basis Development activities undertaken on a not-for-profit basis
Application platform SmartyGrants
Deadline 11 September 2026
Guidelines DAP Guidelines
Administering institution Australian Embassy

The core program information above is based on the Australian Embassy’s published DAP announcement.

Tips for Preparing a Strong Application

Although the source does not prescribe a particular application strategy, applicants can improve the clarity of their proposal by ensuring that the project is presented in a structured and evidence-based manner.

1. Clearly explain the need

Start by explaining the humanitarian or development challenge that the project is designed to address. Avoid vague statements and provide a clear explanation of why intervention is needed.

2. Identify the intended beneficiaries

Describe the community or group that will benefit from the project. Make it clear how the proposed activities respond to their needs.

3. Present realistic activities

A strong small-grants proposal should have activities that are practical and achievable within the available resources and timeframe.

4. Focus on measurable outcomes

Explain what the project is expected to achieve. Where appropriate, identify concrete outputs and outcomes that can demonstrate progress.

5. Demonstrate local relevance

Because DAP is focused on humanitarian and development objectives in Lebanon and Syria, applicants should ensure that the proposed initiative responds to a genuine local need.

6. Follow the funding requirements

This is particularly important. Applicants should carefully review the official DAP Guidelines rather than relying solely on summaries of the opportunity. The Embassy specifically directs applicants to the guidelines for information about the program and funding requirements.

7. Submit before the deadline

The deadline is 11 September 2026. Applicants should allow sufficient time to complete the application and check all information before submission.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Australian Embassy Direct Aid Program?

It is a flexible small-grants program of the Australian Embassy focused on relieving humanitarian hardship and advancing development objectives through projects in Lebanon and Syria.

What category of opportunity is DAP?

The Direct Aid Program is a grant opportunity, specifically a small-grants program.

Who can apply?

The Embassy identifies individuals, community groups and non-governmental organisations engaged in development activities on a not-for-profit basis as applicants whose proposals may be assessed.

Which countries are covered?

The current DAP announcement focuses on development and humanitarian projects in Lebanon and Syria.

Is there a specific race or ethnicity requirement?

The provided source does not specify a race or ethnicity requirement.

Is there an age requirement?

The provided source does not state an age requirement.

Do applicants need a particular academic qualification?

No academic qualification is specified in the provided announcement. Applicants should consult the official DAP Guidelines for the complete requirements.

What is the application deadline?

The deadline is 11 September 2026.

Where do applicants submit their applications?

Applications are submitted through the designated SmartyGrants platform.

Should applicants read the guidelines before applying?

Yes. The Australian Embassy specifically instructs prospective applicants to review the DAP guidelines to understand the program and funding requirements before starting the application.

Visit HERE for more information about the Australian Embassy Direct Aid Program 2026–27.

Conclusion

The Australian Embassy Direct Aid Program 2026–27 provides a funding opportunity for individuals, community groups and non-governmental organisations undertaking not-for-profit development activities in Lebanon and Syria. Its primary focus is on relieving humanitarian hardship and advancing developmental objectives, while ensuring that supported projects are consistent with Australia’s international relations and public diplomacy objectives.

For applicants working on practical humanitarian or development initiatives, the program represents an opportunity to seek support for projects responding to needs within affected communities. The Australian Embassy has also made information about previous funded projects available, giving prospective applicants an additional resource for understanding the program’s history.

The most important step before applying is to read the official DAP Guidelines carefully and verify that the proposed project satisfies the funding requirements. Eligible applicants should then prepare a clear, practical and locally relevant proposal and submit it through the official SmartyGrants platform before the 11 September 2026 deadline.

For more global Grant opportunities, visit OFY HERE.

item.content:encoded:
The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence is creating an urgent need for better ways to evaluate what AI systems can actually accomplish in the real world. While many existing AI benchmarks measure narrow technical capabilities, the next frontier involves understanding whether advanced AI models and autonomous agents can perform economically valuable, complex, multi-hour professional tasks.

The Mercor Research Fellowship — APEX offers researchers and ambitious domain experts an opportunity to contribute directly to this emerging field.

Through the fellowship, selected participants will receive substantial funding, access to frontier AI models, GPU computing resources, expert human-data support, proprietary datasets, mentorship, and the opportunity to work on research that could influence how the global AI industry measures model capabilities.

The program offers a $40,000 stipend for a three-month fellowship or an $80,000 stipend for a six-month fellowship. Fellows can participate remotely or, where appropriate, work in person from Mercor’s San Francisco office.

Unlike a traditional research fellowship where participants join a predefined research project, the Mercor Research Fellowship is built around the applicant’s own research proposal. Applicants are expected to pitch a specific benchmark, evaluation methodology, or economic study they want to develop.

This makes the fellowship particularly attractive for independent researchers and specialists who already have ambitious ideas about how AI systems should be tested, measured, evaluated, or studied.

The application deadline is September 26, 2026, at 9:00 AM GMT+3.

About Mercor

Mercor is an AI-focused company working at the intersection of human expertise, artificial intelligence, data infrastructure, and the future of work.

The company’s mission is to organize human intelligence to power the AI economy. Mercor operates a platform connecting millions of domain experts with opportunities to contribute their knowledge and expertise toward the development and improvement of frontier AI systems.

According to the program information, experts on Mercor’s platform collectively contribute to training frontier AI models across numerous specialized disciplines.

Mercor is building infrastructure that connects human expertise with advanced AI systems. This includes supporting AI companies and enterprises in understanding how professionals perform complex work and translating real-world expertise into data, workflows, evaluations, and AI agents.

The company also works with enterprise organizations, including large corporations, to capture and understand how highly skilled professionals perform their work.

Mercor’s research activities focus heavily on a critical question:

How can researchers accurately determine whether AI systems are capable of performing meaningful real-world professional work?

Answering this question requires more than conventional AI benchmarks. It requires realistic tasks, expert-designed evaluations, reliable grading systems, and careful research into the economic consequences of AI adoption.

This is where Mercor’s APEX research initiative becomes particularly important.

What Is the Mercor APEX Benchmark Family?

The APEX benchmark family is designed to measure whether frontier AI systems can perform economically valuable work in real professional environments.

Rather than focusing exclusively on short questions, coding puzzles, or standardized academic problems, APEX explores complex and realistic tasks that professionals encounter in their daily work.

These can include:

  • Multi-hour agentic tasks in investment banking
  • Corporate law assignments
  • Professional accounting workflows
  • Real-world software engineering problems
  • Graduate-level scientific research tasks
  • Complex financial workflows
  • Long-horizon professional decision-making
  • Research-level mathematics and scientific reasoning

The goal is to move AI evaluation closer to the realities of professional work.

For example, an AI system may perform well on a short multiple-choice examination but struggle when required to independently complete a complex workflow involving multiple applications, ambiguous instructions, iterative decision-making, research, documentation, and professional judgment.

Mercor’s APEX benchmarks aim to investigate these differences.

Importantly, the benchmarks are developed and validated using Mercor’s network of domain experts. These experts can include professionals such as:

  • Lawyers
  • Accountants
  • Software engineers
  • Scientists
  • Consultants
  • Finance professionals
  • Other specialized practitioners

This expert-driven approach helps ensure that the tasks reflect genuine professional work rather than simplified textbook exercises.

About the Mercor Research Fellowship

The Mercor Research Fellowship funds researchers and domain experts who want to build the next generation of AI benchmarks, evaluation techniques, and economic analyses.

The fellowship is structured around an applicant’s research proposal.

Rather than simply applying to join a general research rotation, candidates are expected to identify an important problem and propose a project they want to pursue.

Applicants may pitch ideas such as:

  • A completely new AI benchmark
  • A new domain for evaluating AI capabilities
  • A more difficult task format
  • A new methodology for evaluating AI agents
  • A framework for measuring agent reliability
  • A method for improving benchmark validity
  • A novel grading or scoring methodology
  • An empirical study examining AI’s economic impact
  • Research investigating how AI affects firms and labor markets
  • A study using proprietary data from Mercor’s platform

If selected, fellows receive resources to design, implement, validate, and potentially publish their research.

This includes access to computing infrastructure, expert labor, mentorship, AI models, and research data.

The fellowship therefore provides an opportunity to move from an initial research idea to a completed and validated project.

Research Opportunities in AI Evaluation

One of the major areas supported by the fellowship is AI evaluation.

AI evaluation has become increasingly important as frontier models become more capable. Researchers need reliable methods for determining what models can and cannot do.

However, evaluating advanced AI systems presents several challenges.

A benchmark must answer questions such as:

  • Does the task represent a real-world capability?
  • Is the benchmark sufficiently difficult?
  • Can the benchmark be contaminated by training data?
  • Are grading systems reliable?
  • Do human experts agree with automated evaluation methods?
  • Does high benchmark performance translate into real-world usefulness?
  • Can AI agents perform long-horizon tasks reliably?
  • How should cost and computational resources be incorporated into evaluation?
  • How can researchers distinguish memorization from genuine capability?

The Mercor Research Fellowship encourages fellows to explore these and other important questions.

Successful fellows may design entirely new ways of measuring AI capability.

Research Opportunities in the Economics of AI

In addition to benchmark development, the fellowship supports research examining the economic impact of artificial intelligence.

AI is expected to influence:

  • Employment
  • Labor markets
  • Professional services
  • Business productivity
  • Organizational structures
  • Hiring practices
  • Demand for specialized expertise
  • Firm strategy
  • The structure of work itself

However, measuring these changes requires access to meaningful data.

Mercor’s economics team works to understand how AI is changing the labor market and quantify its broader economic consequences.

The organization has access to unique data sources, including:

  • A marketplace involving millions of candidates
  • Internal AI usage metrics
  • Enterprise data
  • Human expertise and matching data
  • Information related to the supply and demand for professional expertise

Fellows interested in economics can propose empirical studies using these resources.

Potential projects could investigate how AI changes professional work, how organizations adopt AI, how AI-native firms operate, or how human expertise interacts with increasingly capable AI systems.

Mercor Research Fellowship Program Details

The fellowship is designed to provide flexibility while requiring a substantial commitment from participants.

Duration

The fellowship lasts between:

  • Three months, or
  • Six months

Admissions are conducted on a rolling basis.

Commitment

Selected fellows must commit to at least:

30 hours per week

Full-time participation is preferred.

This means the program is intended to be a serious research engagement rather than a casual or part-time extracurricular opportunity.

The fellowship may be suitable for individuals who are:

  • Taking academic leave
  • Completing a summer research project
  • Pursuing a flexible stage of a PhD
  • Transitioning between professional roles
  • Conducting independent research
  • Exploring a career in AI evaluation

Location

The fellowship supports remote participation.

Fellows may also have the opportunity to work in person at Mercor’s San Francisco office.

The flexibility of remote participation makes the program potentially accessible to researchers beyond the organization’s physical office locations, although applicants should carefully review the official application requirements.

Admission Model

One of the most distinctive features of the fellowship is its proposal-based structure.

Applicants do not simply apply for a generic research position.

Instead, they are expected to submit a specific idea for:

  • A benchmark
  • An evaluation methodology
  • An empirical research study

The fellowship is funded around the fellow’s proposed project.

Therefore, the quality, originality, relevance, and feasibility of the research pitch are likely to be important factors in the selection process.

What Will Mercor Research Fellows Do?

Selected fellows will participate in the complete research and development process.

This involves much more than theoretical analysis.

1. Propose and Scope a Research Project

The first major responsibility is identifying a meaningful problem that is not adequately addressed by existing research.

Fellows may propose:

  • New benchmarks
  • Evaluation techniques
  • AI measurement methodologies
  • Economic studies
  • Empirical analyses

A strong project should have a clearly defined scope.

Applicants should ideally demonstrate:

  • Why the problem matters
  • What existing research is missing
  • How the proposed work differs from existing benchmarks
  • What methodology will be used
  • What resources are required
  • What outcomes the project could produce

The ability to transform an ambitious idea into a practical research project will be particularly valuable.

2. Build and Validate AI Benchmarks

For fellows working on benchmark development, the work may involve several stages.

These include:

Designing Task Specifications

Researchers may need to determine what tasks AI models should complete.

Tasks should ideally reflect meaningful and realistic professional challenges.

Developing Grading Rubrics

A benchmark requires reliable ways to evaluate performance.

Fellows may develop detailed rubrics that define:

  • What constitutes successful performance
  • What common errors look like
  • How partial success should be measured
  • How human experts should assess outputs

Working With Domain Experts

Mercor provides access to a network of vetted experts.

Depending on the project, fellows may collaborate with professionals such as:

  • Lawyers
  • Engineers
  • Accountants
  • Scientists
  • Consultants

These experts can help ensure that tasks accurately represent professional workflows.

Piloting Tasks

Before releasing a benchmark, researchers may need to test tasks.

Piloting helps identify problems such as:

  • Ambiguous instructions
  • Unrealistic assumptions
  • Inconsistent grading
  • Tasks that are too easy
  • Tasks that are excessively difficult
  • Poor alignment with real-world work

Calibrating Scoring Systems

Researchers may compare evaluation approaches and refine scoring methodologies.

The objective is to ensure that benchmark scores provide meaningful information about actual AI capability.

Testing Frontier AI Models

Fellows may run advanced AI models against their benchmarks.

This can help researchers identify:

  • Where models succeed
  • Where models fail
  • What types of reasoning remain difficult
  • How performance varies across tasks
  • Whether models can complete long-horizon workflows

3. Conduct Economic Research

Fellows working on economics may conduct a wide variety of empirical research projects.

Potential activities could include:

  • Designing field experiments
  • Studying expert behavior
  • Analyzing labor market data
  • Investigating enterprise AI adoption
  • Examining productivity changes
  • Studying supply and demand dynamics
  • Conducting quantitative analyses
  • Investigating organizational transformation

The research may use Mercor’s proprietary datasets, subject to internal review and appropriate access requirements.

4. Publish and Share Research Findings

The fellowship aims to produce tangible research outputs.

Depending on the project, fellows may produce:

  • Academic papers
  • Research reports
  • Open datasets
  • New AI benchmarks
  • Public leaderboards
  • Evaluation methodologies
  • Internal research frameworks

Researchers may also collaborate with Mercor’s research and engineering teams to integrate findings into future projects.

This creates an opportunity for fellows to contribute work that could have practical influence beyond the duration of the fellowship.

Mercor Research Fellowship Focus Areas

Mercor has identified several areas of particular interest.

However, applicants are not restricted to these topics.

Strong proposals outside the listed areas are also encouraged.

Long-Horizon Agentic Tasks in Professional Services

AI agents are increasingly expected to perform tasks that involve multiple steps and extended periods of autonomous work.

Mercor is interested in evaluating long-horizon tasks in professional services such as:

  • Law
  • Finance
  • Consulting

This work may extend the organization’s existing APEX-Agents research.

Researchers could investigate how AI systems perform when tasks require:

  • Planning
  • Research
  • Tool usage
  • Decision-making
  • Iteration
  • Error correction
  • Long-term context management

Real-World Software Engineering Evaluation

Software engineering evaluation is another major focus area.

Traditional coding benchmarks often focus on isolated programming problems.

However, professional software development involves significantly more complex workflows.

Potential research may explore:

  • Codebase navigation
  • Software architecture
  • Debugging
  • Testing
  • Documentation
  • Multi-file development
  • Long-term engineering tasks

This focus area aims to move beyond narrow issue-resolution benchmarks.

Professional Accounting and Finance Workflows

AI systems are increasingly being tested on finance and accounting tasks.

Mercor is interested in developing more realistic evaluations involving professional workflows.

Potential areas could include:

  • Financial analysis
  • Accounting procedures
  • Reporting
  • Auditing workflows
  • Financial modeling
  • Business decision-making

The objective is to understand whether AI can reliably perform economically valuable professional work.

AI for Science Evaluations

AI has the potential to accelerate scientific research.

However, evaluating scientific AI capabilities remains challenging.

The fellowship supports research involving areas such as:

  • Research-level mathematics
  • Biology
  • Materials science
  • Theoretical physics

Researchers may investigate how AI systems perform on complex scientific reasoning and research tasks.

New Economic Benchmarks

Some economically valuable skills do not easily fit into conventional AI benchmarks.

Mercor is interested in developing evaluations for capabilities such as:

  • Negotiation
  • Management
  • Professional decision-making
  • Other economically significant skills

These areas are difficult to evaluate because performance may depend on context, interaction, and long-term outcomes.

Researchers may therefore develop entirely new benchmark formats.

Novel AI Evaluation Methodologies

Applicants can also focus on improving the science of evaluation itself.

Potential topics include:

Contamination Resistance

Researchers may investigate ways to ensure that AI benchmarks are not compromised by models having previously encountered benchmark data during training.

Rubric Design

A strong evaluation depends on reliable criteria.

Researchers may develop improved methods for creating and validating grading rubrics.

Human-versus-Model Grading Agreement

An important research question is whether automated evaluation systems agree with human experts.

Researchers could study:

  • Inter-rater reliability
  • Automated grading accuracy
  • Human expert disagreement
  • Hybrid evaluation systems

Cost-Adjusted Scoring

Different AI systems may require vastly different computational resources.

Researchers may investigate how performance should be measured alongside:

  • Computational cost
  • API expenses
  • Time requirements
  • Human intervention

Economics of Human Data Platforms

Mercor is also interested in research examining platforms that connect human expertise with AI development.

Possible topics include:

  • Pricing
  • Labor matching
  • Supply elasticity
  • Demand elasticity
  • Marketplace dynamics
  • Expert incentives

This research could contribute to a deeper understanding of how human intelligence becomes part of the AI economy.

AI Theory of the Firm

Another important research area involves understanding what an AI-native organization looks like.

As AI becomes integrated into organizations, fundamental questions emerge:

  • How will firms organize work?
  • Which tasks will remain human-led?
  • How will AI agents interact with employees?
  • How will management structures change?
  • How will productivity be measured?
  • What new business models will emerge?

Researchers interested in empirical studies of AI-native organizations may find this focus area particularly relevant.

Who Should Apply for the Mercor Research Fellowship?

The fellowship is designed for individuals who are genuinely interested in AI evaluation and research.

Mercor specifically emphasizes that evaluation should not simply be viewed as a temporary stepping stone toward model-building roles.

Successful applicants should demonstrate a genuine intellectual interest in questions surrounding measurement, benchmarking, reliability, and AI capability assessment.

Applicants may have backgrounds in:

  • Economics
  • Computer Science
  • Machine Learning
  • Artificial Intelligence
  • Statistics
  • Measurement
  • Psychometrics
  • Human-Computer Interaction
  • Social Science
  • Other adjacent disciplines

The program may also be valuable for domain experts with specialized knowledge.

Bonus experience may include expertise in:

  • Agentic AI evaluation
  • Reinforcement learning environments
  • Law
  • Finance
  • Medicine
  • Scientific research

Key Qualities Mercor Is Looking For

Applicants should demonstrate several important characteristics.

A Genuine Interest in AI Evaluation

Candidates should be interested in the scientific challenge of determining how AI capabilities should be measured.

This involves thinking critically about:

  • Benchmark design
  • Measurement validity
  • Reliability
  • Real-world relevance
  • Evaluation methodology

A Strong Research Background

Applicants should have relevant academic, technical, or professional experience.

However, interdisciplinary expertise may also be valuable.

For example, a legal professional with strong knowledge of AI could potentially propose a benchmark evaluating complex legal workflows.

Similarly, an economist could propose a study examining how AI changes labor market behavior.

A Specific Research Idea

Perhaps the most important requirement is having a concrete project proposal.

Applicants should be prepared to explain:

  • What they want to build or study
  • Why it matters
  • What gap it addresses
  • How they would approach the project
  • What resources may be required

A generic interest in AI research alone may not be sufficient.

Ability to Work Independently

The fellowship operates in a fast-paced environment.

Participants should be comfortable with:

  • Rapid iteration
  • Independent decision-making
  • Direct feedback
  • Working with real-world research problems
  • Managing ambiguity

The program may provide less structured guidance than a traditional academic laboratory.

Significant Time Commitment

Applicants must be able to commit at least 30 hours per week.

Full-time participation is preferred.

Candidates should therefore ensure they have sufficient availability before applying.

Mercor Research Fellowship Compensation

One of the major benefits of the fellowship is its competitive financial support.

Selected fellows can receive either:

  • $40,000 for a three-month fellowship, or
  • $80,000 for a six-month fellowship

The stipend structure provides significant support for researchers who want to dedicate substantial time to an ambitious project.

The fellowship is therefore positioned as an opportunity for individuals who want to seriously invest in independent AI evaluation or economic research.

Benefits of the Mercor Research Fellowship

In addition to financial compensation, fellows receive access to significant research resources.

1. Unlimited API Credits

Fellows receive access to API credits that can support experimentation with AI systems.

This can be especially valuable for researchers conducting large-scale model evaluations.

2. Dedicated GPU Computing Budget

Selected participants receive resources for GPU compute.

This enables researchers to conduct computationally intensive experiments.

3. Paid Expert and Human-Data Support

Researchers may receive access to paid expert labor and human-data resources.

This is particularly valuable for benchmark development because high-quality professional evaluations often require specialized human expertise.

4. Weekly Individual Mentorship

Fellows receive weekly one-on-one mentorship from members of the APEX research team.

This provides an opportunity to receive feedback and guidance throughout the project.

5. Access to Mercor’s Research Organization

Participants may interact with the broader Mercor research ecosystem.

This can expose fellows to researchers and practitioners working at the intersection of AI, economics, evaluation, and professional expertise.

6. Access to Marketplace and Expert-Network Data

Subject to appropriate review, fellows may access data that can support empirical research.

This creates opportunities for research projects that may not be possible using publicly available datasets alone.

7. Access to Frontier AI Models

Participants may receive access to frontier model APIs.

This enables fellows to test and compare advanced AI systems.

8. Internal Evaluation Infrastructure

Researchers may be able to use Mercor’s internal evaluation tools and infrastructure.

This can significantly reduce the technical barriers involved in building sophisticated benchmarks.

9. Real Enterprise Evaluation Problems

Where appropriate, fellows may gain exposure to real evaluation problems involving enterprise customers.

This can help ensure that research remains connected to practical challenges.

10. Optional San Francisco Workspace

Fellows interested in working in person may have access to a desk at Mercor’s San Francisco office.

11. Professional Research Network

Participants may receive introductions to Mercor’s network of researchers across:

  • Frontier AI laboratories
  • Academia
  • Research organizations

Networking opportunities can be particularly valuable for researchers interested in building long-term careers in AI evaluation.

12. Potential Full-Time Employment Opportunity

Outstanding fellows may be considered for a full-time position on Mercor’s APEX research team after completing the fellowship.

This creates a potential pathway from fellowship participation into a longer-term research role.

How to Develop a Strong Fellowship Proposal

Because the fellowship is built around the applicant’s pitch, prospective applicants should dedicate significant effort to developing a compelling research proposal.

A strong proposal should ideally include the following elements.

Define a Clear Problem

Begin by identifying a meaningful gap.

Ask questions such as:

  • What is currently missing from AI evaluation?
  • What professional capability is poorly measured?
  • What existing benchmark limitation needs to be addressed?
  • What economic question lacks sufficient empirical evidence?

Explain Why the Problem Matters

A proposal should demonstrate significance.

Explain how the project could contribute to:

  • AI safety
  • AI reliability
  • Scientific measurement
  • Economic understanding
  • Professional AI deployment
  • Benchmark development

Present a Practical Methodology

Describe how the research will be conducted.

This could include:

  • Experimental design
  • Data collection
  • Expert interviews
  • Benchmark construction
  • Statistical analysis
  • Model testing

Keep the Scope Realistic

The project should be ambitious but achievable within three to six months.

Applicants should avoid proposing a project that is too broad to complete.

Identify Expected Outputs

Consider what the project could produce.

Possible outputs include:

  • A research paper
  • A benchmark
  • An open dataset
  • A leaderboard
  • An evaluation methodology
  • An empirical study

Demonstrate Relevant Expertise

Applicants should explain why they are well-positioned to conduct the proposed work.

Relevant experience could include:

  • Previous research
  • Technical expertise
  • Industry knowledge
  • Domain specialization
  • Statistical experience
  • AI development experience

How to Apply for the Mercor Research Fellowship

Interested applicants should submit their application through the official Mercor application portal.

Applicants should be prepared to present a specific research idea involving:

  • A benchmark
  • An evaluation methodology
  • An empirical study

Because the fellowship is centered around the applicant’s proposal, candidates should carefully refine their project idea before submitting an application.

Applicants should ensure their proposal demonstrates:

  1. A clearly defined research problem.
  2. The significance of the problem.
  3. A practical research methodology.
  4. A realistic project scope.
  5. Relevant expertise or experience.
  6. The potential impact of the proposed work.

Application Links

Applicants can learn more about the fellowship and submit their applications through the official Mercor portal.

APPLY HERE

Important Deadline

The deadline to apply for the Mercor Research Fellowship — APEX is:

September 26, 2026, at 9:00 AM GMT+3

Applicants should avoid waiting until the final hours before submitting their application, particularly because a strong application requires a carefully developed research pitch.

Since the fellowship operates with rolling admissions, submitting a well-prepared application early may also be beneficial.

Why the Mercor Research Fellowship Is a Unique Opportunity

The Mercor Research Fellowship stands out because it combines several elements that are not commonly available together in a single research program.

Participants receive:

  • Significant financial support
  • Flexibility to propose their own research
  • Access to frontier AI systems
  • GPU computing resources
  • Human expert support
  • Individual mentorship
  • Proprietary research data
  • Real-world enterprise evaluation problems
  • Opportunities to publish meaningful work
  • Potential pathways toward full-time research positions

Most importantly, the fellowship allows researchers to work on one of the most important emerging questions in artificial intelligence:

How do we know whether increasingly powerful AI systems can perform meaningful, economically valuable work in the real world?

As AI models move beyond answering questions and generating text toward operating as autonomous agents, traditional evaluation methods may become increasingly insufficient.

The need for better benchmarks, stronger evaluation methodologies, and rigorous economic research is therefore likely to grow significantly.

Researchers who want to contribute to this emerging field have an opportunity to develop ambitious projects with substantial institutional and technical support.

Visit HERE to learn more about the Mercor Research Fellowship APEX 2026.

Conclusion

The Mercor Research Fellowship — APEX 2026 presents a highly competitive opportunity for researchers, economists, AI practitioners, computer scientists, statisticians, domain experts, and interdisciplinary thinkers interested in the future of artificial intelligence evaluation and the economics of AI.

With funding of up to $80,000, access to advanced computing infrastructure, frontier AI models, expert networks, proprietary data, and direct mentorship from the APEX research team, the fellowship provides selected participants with the resources needed to transform an ambitious research idea into a meaningful project.

The program’s proposal-driven model makes it particularly suitable for individuals who already have a clear idea about a benchmark they want to build, an evaluation challenge they want to solve, or an economic question about AI they want to investigate.

Whether the proposed work focuses on long-horizon AI agents, software engineering, law, finance, accounting, scientific reasoning, AI evaluation methodology, labor markets, or the future structure of AI-native firms, Mercor is looking for strong ideas that can advance understanding of AI’s real-world capabilities and economic consequences.

For researchers seeking to work at the intersection of artificial intelligence, measurement, professional expertise, and economic transformation, the Mercor Research Fellowship offers an opportunity to conduct impactful work while receiving substantial financial and technical support.

Interested candidates should develop a focused and compelling research proposal and submit their applications before the deadline of September 26, 2026, at 9:00 AM GMT+3.

Mycelia Fellowship 2026: An Opportunity for Ethical Storytelling Practitioners

The Social Resonance Lab (SRL) Mycelia Fellowship 2026 is an exciting new opportunity designed to support practitioners working at the intersection of storytelling, arts, humanities, civic participation, technology, community engagement, and intersectional practice.

The inaugural fellowship cohort will select two fellows whose existing projects demonstrate innovative approaches to ethical storytelling. Rather than supporting entirely new ideas that have not yet begun, the Mycelia Fellowship focuses on strengthening, documenting, refining, extending, or scaling projects that are already underway.

Selected fellows will receive a $2,000 stipend alongside direct advisory support from the Social Resonance Lab team. Participants will also gain opportunities to increase the visibility of their work, share their knowledge with wider audiences, contribute to discussions on ethical storytelling, and engage with other practitioners working across creative, civic, technological, and community-centered spaces.

The fellowship is built around an important idea: stories do not exist in isolation. Stories travel between people, communities, generations, technologies, and institutions. As they move, they can change shape, acquire new meanings, and influence how individuals and communities are understood.

Through the Mycelia Fellowship, participants will be encouraged to explore important questions surrounding storytelling, including who has the power to tell stories, who receives recognition when stories are adapted, what responsibilities storytellers have toward communities, and how ethical practices can be maintained when narratives continuously evolve.

The application deadline for the inaugural Mycelia Fellowship cohort is September 13, 2026, at 11:59 PM.

About the Social Resonance Lab

The Mycelia Fellowship is organized by the Social Resonance Lab, a collaborative research studio focused on understanding how ethical storytelling can contribute to stronger human connection.

Through creative inquiry, partnerships, research, experimentation, and collaboration, Social Resonance Lab explores how stories can be developed and shared in ways that promote:

  • Human connection
  • Empathy
  • Trust
  • Community understanding
  • Ethical representation
  • Shared learning
  • Creative collaboration
  • Responsible narrative practices

The organization’s work recognizes that storytelling is not simply about producing compelling narratives. Stories influence public understanding, shape collective memory, affect political and social perceptions, and determine whose experiences become visible or invisible.

For this reason, ethical storytelling requires practitioners to think critically about issues such as:

  • Power
  • Representation
  • Attribution
  • Ownership
  • Consent
  • Community relationships
  • Narrative responsibility
  • Technology
  • Digital platforms
  • Algorithmic influence

The Mycelia Fellowship provides a structured environment for practitioners to investigate these issues while advancing their existing projects.

Understanding the Concept Behind the Mycelia Fellowship

The fellowship takes inspiration from mycelium, the complex underground network of fungal structures that connects and supports ecosystems.

Mycelium operates largely beneath the surface, creating interconnected networks that allow nutrients and information to move throughout an ecosystem. Social Resonance Lab uses this concept as a metaphor for storytelling.

Stories, like mycelial networks, rarely exist independently.

A story may:

  • Originate from an individual experience
  • Be shared within a family or community
  • Be documented by researchers
  • Be adapted by artists
  • Spread through digital platforms
  • Be transformed by audiences
  • Influence political conversations
  • Become part of collective memory

As stories move between people and contexts, important ethical questions emerge.

For example:

  • Who should receive credit for a story?
  • What happens when someone else’s story is retold?
  • How should storytellers acknowledge the communities from which narratives originate?
  • What responsibilities exist when adapting historical or community narratives?
  • How can storytelling avoid exploitation?
  • How do digital technologies influence ownership and attribution?
  • What happens when algorithms amplify some stories while suppressing others?

The Mycelia Fellowship encourages fellows to examine storytelling as a living and interconnected ecosystem.

Participants are expected to understand that individual creative work can have broader consequences. A story can influence communities far beyond its original context. Therefore, practitioners must consider both the opportunities and responsibilities associated with storytelling.

The fellowship emphasizes the idea that practitioners are simultaneously:

  1. Influenced by broader storytelling ecosystems.
  2. Contributors to those ecosystems.
  3. Responsible for the impacts their storytelling practices may create.

Through this framework, the fellowship seeks to transform individual artistic, archival, civic, and technological initiatives into work capable of generating sustained collective impact.

What Is the Purpose of the Mycelia Fellowship?

The primary goal of the Mycelia Fellowship is to support innovative practitioners advancing ethical storytelling interventions.

The fellowship provides several forms of support designed to help participants deepen and strengthen their work.

These include:

1. Financial Support

Each selected fellow will receive a stipend of $2,000.

The financial support is intended to help practitioners continue advancing work that is already underway.

Unlike programs that require participants to create completely new projects, the Mycelia Fellowship recognizes that meaningful projects often require additional support to:

  • Expand their reach
  • Improve documentation
  • Develop stronger strategies
  • Refine methodologies
  • Increase visibility
  • Strengthen community engagement
  • Explore new applications
  • Build sustainable approaches

2. Professional Advising and Consultancy

Selected fellows will receive direct support from the Social Resonance Lab team.

Areas of expertise available to fellows include:

  • Project management
  • Evaluation
  • Communications
  • Design
  • Community storytelling

This advisory support can help fellows think strategically about the development and future direction of their projects.

For practitioners working independently or within small organizations, access to specialized expertise can be particularly valuable.

The consultancy component of the fellowship may help participants better understand how to:

  • Organize and manage projects
  • Evaluate impact
  • Communicate complex ideas
  • Present work to different audiences
  • Strengthen storytelling strategies
  • Improve public engagement
  • Document learning
  • Build sustainable practices

3. Visibility and Knowledge-Sharing Opportunities

The Mycelia Fellowship also provides fellows with opportunities to share their work publicly.

This is an important component because the program is not only focused on supporting individual projects. It also aims to contribute to broader conversations surrounding ethical storytelling.

Fellows will have opportunities to share their experiences, methodologies, insights, and learning with:

  • Other practitioners
  • Researchers
  • Creative professionals
  • Community members
  • Storytelling organizations
  • Public audiences

By creating spaces for knowledge exchange, the fellowship seeks to advance broader field practice.

Mycelia Fellowship 2026 Duration and Structure

The inaugural Mycelia Fellowship will run for eight weeks.

Fellowship Period

November 1 – December 31, 2026

Cohort Size

Only two fellows will be selected.

The small cohort structure may provide participants with opportunities for more direct engagement and personalized support.

Fellowship Format

The fellowship will be conducted remotely.

Activities will include:

  • A lightweight virtual kickoff
  • Semi-regular check-ins
  • Advisory support
  • Collaborative discussions
  • Presentations
  • Knowledge-sharing activities

Because the program is remote, fellows will not need to relocate for the fellowship. However, applicants must meet the residency and payment requirements outlined by the organizers.

Mycelia Fellowship Stipend and Benefits

Each selected fellow will receive a $2,000 stipend.

In addition to the financial award, fellows will benefit from professional support and opportunities for public engagement.

Key benefits include:

Financial Support

  • $2,000 stipend per fellow

Professional Advising

Support from the Social Resonance Lab team in areas such as:

  • Project management
  • Evaluation
  • Communications
  • Design
  • Community storytelling

Increased Visibility

Fellows will have opportunities to share their work and insights through SRL platforms and public-facing activities.

Professional Development

Participants can further develop their thinking and practice around:

  • Ethical storytelling
  • Community engagement
  • Narrative responsibility
  • Power dynamics
  • Intersectional practice
  • Digital storytelling
  • Civic participation
  • Technology and storytelling

Knowledge Exchange

Fellows will engage with other practitioners and audiences interested in ethical storytelling and related fields.

Platform for Public Engagement

Selected participants will have opportunities to present their work and participate in conversations with the public.

Required Deliverables for Mycelia Fellows

Selected fellows will be expected to complete a short set of shared deliverables during the fellowship period.

These deliverables are designed to help participants document their work, share insights, and contribute to broader discussions about ethical storytelling.

1. Written Contribution to the SRL Substack

Each fellow will produce one written piece for the Social Resonance Lab Substack.

This contribution may provide fellows with an opportunity to:

  • Document their project
  • Share research insights
  • Reflect on ethical storytelling practices
  • Introduce audiences to their work
  • Discuss challenges and lessons
  • Contribute to public conversations

Strong writing skills will therefore be particularly valuable for applicants.

2. Podcast Participation

Fellows will participate as guests in an episode of Social Resonance Lab’s upcoming podcast series focused on ethical storytelling.

The podcast opportunity will allow fellows to discuss their projects and perspectives with wider audiences.

Participants may have an opportunity to share:

  • Their professional journey
  • Their project methodology
  • Key challenges
  • Ethical questions
  • Community experiences
  • Lessons learned
  • Future directions

3. Co-Leading a Workshop

Each fellow will participate in a workshop activity.

The workshop will involve:

  • Co-leading a session
  • Delivering a 30-minute presentation
  • Presenting their work
  • Engaging in dialogue with practitioners
  • Participating in discussions with SRL
  • Interacting with public audiences

This component means successful applicants should be comfortable communicating their ideas and engaging with diverse audiences.

Thematic Tracks of the Mycelia Fellowship

Applicants must identify which thematic track best aligns with their project.

The fellowship contains two major thematic tracks:

  1. Arts as a Civic Tool
  2. AI and the Digital Landscape

Both tracks share an interest in ethical storytelling, intersectional practice, and power dynamics.

Importantly, the fellowship considers not only how stories are produced but also how they are experienced by audiences and communities directly affected by the narratives.

Track A: Arts as a Civic Tool

The first thematic track focuses on the use of art and narrative as forms of civic participation.

Projects under this track explore how artistic and storytelling practices can contribute to public engagement and responses to social issues.

The fellowship is particularly interested in work that represents ongoing and complex forms of:

  • Injustice
  • Resistance
  • Identity
  • Social transformation
  • Civic participation
  • Community engagement

Rather than reducing complex issues to simplified narratives with clear resolutions, Track A encourages projects that recognize the ongoing nature of social and political experiences.

This is especially relevant to issues sometimes described as “slow” forms of injustice.

These may involve challenges that develop gradually or persist over long periods, making them difficult to communicate through traditional storytelling formats.

Projects can explore how art and storytelling help communities understand and engage with such issues.

Examples of Projects Suitable for Track A

Potential projects may include:

Phygital Civic Activities

Projects that connect physical and digital participation while linking democratic engagement with artistic practice.

Examples could include initiatives involving:

  • Community art
  • Digital storytelling
  • Local democracy projects
  • Interactive public engagement
  • Hyperlocal creative participation

Artistic Responses to Local Issues

Projects that engage with specific local challenges through creative and humanities-based approaches.

These may include:

  • Community storytelling initiatives
  • Public art projects
  • Participatory cultural activities
  • Creative research
  • Narrative-based advocacy

Creative Placemaking

Digital campaigns or creative initiatives centered around clearly defined geographic communities within the United States.

These projects may explore how storytelling and creativity contribute to:

  • Community identity
  • Local engagement
  • Public participation
  • Cultural preservation
  • Civic dialogue

Track B: AI and the Digital Landscape

The second thematic track focuses on the relationship between technology, storytelling, power, collective memory, and political agency.

This track is particularly interested in projects that critically examine how:

  • Digital infrastructures
  • Artificial intelligence
  • Algorithms
  • Social media
  • Data systems
  • Platform governance
  • Digital surveillance

shape human narratives and social experiences.

The fellowship does not treat technology as neutral.

Instead, Track B encourages applicants to examine the real-world consequences of data-driven systems.

Technology increasingly influences:

  • Which stories become visible
  • Which voices are amplified
  • Which narratives are suppressed
  • How historical information is preserved
  • How misinformation spreads
  • How communities communicate
  • How personal data is collected
  • How digital surveillance affects communities

Projects under this track should critically investigate these dynamics.

Examples of Projects Suitable for Track B

Eligible or relevant projects may include the following.

Digital Archives and Oral History Projects

Projects documenting community histories while addressing challenges associated with automated moderation or content suppression.

Such initiatives may explore how digital platforms influence historical preservation.

Counter-Surveillance Documentation Tools

Projects documenting how communities navigate surveillance and information control.

Examples could include research or tools examining:

  • Encrypted communication
  • Informal information networks
  • Digital security practices
  • Community communication strategies

Community-Led Data Preservation

Projects that protect local knowledge and narratives from algorithmic erasure.

These initiatives may focus on preserving:

  • Community histories
  • Cultural knowledge
  • Oral traditions
  • Local archives
  • Marginalized narratives

Creative Storytelling Platforms

Projects that help communities maintain control over their narratives in environments shaped by digital oversight and platform power.

These projects may investigate how communities can preserve narrative autonomy when interacting with large technology platforms and algorithmic systems.

Research Questions Driving the Fellowship

The Mycelia Fellowship is grounded in a broader research agenda focused on ethical storytelling.

The central research question is:

How do power dynamics shape who gets to tell stories and how those stories are received?

This question recognizes that storytelling is influenced by unequal access to:

  • Media platforms
  • Financial resources
  • Technology
  • Institutional recognition
  • Cultural authority
  • Publishing opportunities
  • Political influence

The fellowship encourages practitioners to investigate these dynamics through their existing work.

Arts as a Civic Tool Research Question

Applicants under Track A are encouraged to consider:

What methods can organizations and creators use to practice ethics in their storytelling?

This question invites practitioners to explore practical approaches to responsible storytelling.

Potential areas of exploration include:

  • Community participation
  • Consent
  • Attribution
  • Collaborative authorship
  • Representation
  • Long-term community relationships
  • Responsible documentation
  • Participatory creative processes

AI and the Digital Landscape Research Question

Applicants under Track B are encouraged to investigate:

How does the digital landscape, including social media, AI-generated content, and virality, complicate or enable ethical storytelling?

This research question is increasingly relevant as artificial intelligence and algorithmic platforms influence the production and distribution of information.

Potential areas for exploration include:

  • AI-generated narratives
  • Algorithmic bias
  • Digital misinformation
  • Viral storytelling
  • Platform moderation
  • Content suppression
  • Digital memory
  • Automated representation
  • Narrative manipulation

Who Should Apply for the Mycelia Fellowship?

The fellowship is intended for individuals who are already actively engaged in storytelling or arts and humanities work.

The organizers are not seeking applicants who simply have an idea for a completely new initiative.

Instead, they want to support projects that are already in progress and have the potential to be:

  • Scaled
  • Documented
  • Extended
  • Strengthened
  • Refined

Ideal applicants are likely to have experience in fields such as:

  • Storytelling
  • Arts
  • Humanities
  • Creative practice
  • Research
  • Community organizing
  • Movement building
  • Civic engagement
  • Digital culture
  • Archives
  • Oral history
  • Technology and society
  • Ethical communications

Mycelia Fellowship 2026 Eligibility Requirements

Applicants must meet several important eligibility criteria.

1. Applicants Must Have Existing Work in Progress

The fellowship supports practitioners who are already advancing storytelling or arts-humanities projects.

Applicants should therefore demonstrate evidence that they have already begun meaningful work.

The fellowship is suitable for projects seeking:

  • Expansion
  • Documentation
  • Scaling
  • Extension
  • Refinement

Completely new projects developed from scratch are not the primary focus of this opportunity.

2. Applicants Must Demonstrate Intersectional Practice

The fellowship is specifically interested in storytelling and arts-humanities work grounded in intersectional practice.

Applicants should demonstrate awareness of how multiple social identities and systems of power influence human experiences and storytelling.

3. Strong Writing Skills Are Important

Selected fellows will be required to produce a written piece for the SRL Substack.

Applicants should therefore demonstrate strong abilities in:

  • Writing
  • Research
  • Analysis
  • Communication
  • Critical thinking

4. Applicants Should Be Skilled Researchers or Practitioners

The fellowship seeks people capable of exploring complex questions with nuance.

Strong applicants may demonstrate experience in:

  • Research
  • Creative inquiry
  • Documentation
  • Community engagement
  • Storytelling practice
  • Arts and humanities work

5. Applicants Should Demonstrate Leadership

The fellowship seeks practitioners capable of independently advancing projects.

Applicants should demonstrate the ability to:

  • Lead initiatives
  • Manage responsibilities
  • Work independently
  • Develop ideas
  • Complete projects
  • Engage communities

6. Applicants Must Be United States Residents

The fellowship is currently only open to residents of the United States.

Applicants must be based within:

  • The United States
  • US Territories

The application specifically states that fellowship activities must be based domestically.

7. Applicants Must Meet Payment Requirements

Successful fellows must be able to:

  • File a W-9 form
  • Receive stipend payments
  • Access a domestic United States bank account

Applicants who cannot meet these requirements may not be eligible for the fellowship.

How Applications Will Be Evaluated

Applications will be assessed according to several criteria.

Understanding these criteria can help prospective applicants prepare stronger submissions.

Creativity

Applicants will be evaluated based on the originality of their approach and voice.

Strong applications should demonstrate:

  • Innovative thinking
  • Original approaches
  • Creative methodologies
  • Distinct perspectives

Leadership

Applicants should demonstrate their ability to independently lead and advance their projects.

The selection committee will likely consider:

  • Previous leadership experience
  • Initiative
  • Project ownership
  • Ability to execute ideas

Evidence of Prior Execution

Because the fellowship focuses on existing work, applicants must demonstrate evidence of previous or ongoing execution.

Strong evidence may include:

  • Completed projects
  • Ongoing initiatives
  • Research
  • Publications
  • Community programs
  • Digital platforms
  • Archives
  • Creative works
  • Campaigns

Understanding of the SRL Research Agenda

Applicants should demonstrate familiarity with the fellowship’s central themes.

This includes understanding questions related to:

  • Ethical storytelling
  • Power
  • Narrative responsibility
  • Intersectionality
  • Technology
  • Community engagement
  • Attribution
  • Digital storytelling

Fit With a Thematic Track

Applicants must demonstrate a strong connection between their project and either:

  • Arts as a Civic Tool, or
  • AI and the Digital Landscape

Applicants should clearly explain why their work fits within their selected track.

Mycelia Fellowship 2026 Timeline and Key Dates

Applicants should pay close attention to the fellowship timeline.

Application Window Opens

August 31, 2026

Application Deadline

September 13, 2026, at 11:59 PM

Review Period

September 14 – September 27, 2026

Interviews

Late September to Early October 2026

Final Selections Announced

October 23, 2026

Fellow Onboarding

October 27, 2026

Fellowship Period

November – December 2026

More specifically, the fellowship will run from:

November 1 – December 31, 2026

Because only two fellows will be selected, interested applicants should ensure that their applications clearly demonstrate the strength, progress, and relevance of their existing projects.

How to Prepare a Strong Mycelia Fellowship Application

Given the highly selective nature of the fellowship and the small cohort size, applicants should carefully prepare their submissions.

Here are several strategies that may strengthen an application.

1. Clearly Explain Your Existing Project

Since the fellowship does not primarily fund brand-new ideas, applicants should provide clear evidence that their work is already underway.

Explain:

  • What your project is
  • When it began
  • What you have accomplished
  • Who the project serves
  • What challenges exist
  • What the next stage of development involves

2. Demonstrate Ethical Storytelling Practice

Applicants should go beyond simply describing their project.

They should explain how their work engages with ethical questions.

Consider discussing:

  • Community relationships
  • Consent
  • Representation
  • Attribution
  • Ownership
  • Power dynamics
  • Accountability

3. Select the Most Appropriate Track

Applicants should carefully determine whether their project fits better under:

  • Arts as a Civic Tool, or
  • AI and the Digital Landscape

Avoid forcing a project into a track.

Instead, clearly explain the relationship between your existing work and the fellowship’s thematic focus.

4. Provide Evidence of Execution

Selection criteria emphasize evidence of prior execution.

Applicants should highlight tangible examples of their work.

Depending on the project, this could include:

  • Publications
  • Research findings
  • Websites
  • Digital archives
  • Community events
  • Artistic work
  • Campaigns
  • Workshops
  • Documentation

5. Demonstrate Independent Leadership

Explain your specific role in the project.

The fellowship seeks practitioners capable of independently advancing their work.

Applicants should demonstrate:

  • Initiative
  • Decision-making
  • Project ownership
  • Leadership
  • Problem-solving

6. Connect Your Work to the Research Questions

A strong application should demonstrate that the applicant understands the fellowship’s intellectual focus.

Consider how your work addresses:

  • Who gets to tell stories
  • Who controls narratives
  • How stories are received
  • How technology influences storytelling
  • How ethical practices can be strengthened

7. Highlight Your Writing and Communication Skills

Since fellows must write for the SRL Substack and participate in public discussions, applicants should demonstrate strong communication abilities.

Experience in the following areas may be relevant:

  • Writing
  • Public speaking
  • Research communication
  • Workshop facilitation
  • Community engagement

Important Privacy Considerations for Applicants

Applicants submitting information to Social Resonance Lab should understand how personal information may be handled.

According to the organization’s privacy policy, information collected may include:

Information Provided Directly

Such as:

  • Names
  • Email addresses
  • Contact details
  • Fellowship application information

Usage Information

Website-related information may include:

  • IP addresses
  • Browser information
  • Website interaction data

Voluntary Submissions

This may include:

  • Survey responses
  • Research participation
  • Stories voluntarily shared with the organization

The organization states that personal information is not sold, rented, or traded.

Information may be used for purposes such as:

  • Communicating about programs
  • Processing applications
  • Improving websites and content
  • Conducting research
  • Analysis and reporting

Applicants may also have rights to access, correct, or request deletion of personal information depending on applicable laws and circumstances.

How to Apply for the Mycelia Fellowship 2026

Interested and eligible applicants should complete the official Mycelia Fellowship application form before the deadline.

Applicants should carefully review the full program overview before submitting their responses.

The application will ask candidates to provide information including their:

  • Email address
  • City or town of residence
  • US State or Territory of residence
  • Professional background
  • Existing project
  • Thematic track alignment
  • Experience and qualifications

Before submitting an application, candidates should ensure that they:

  1. Meet all residency requirements.
  2. Have an existing project already in progress.
  3. Select the appropriate thematic track.
  4. Demonstrate evidence of prior execution.
  5. Explain their approach to ethical storytelling.
  6. Highlight leadership and research abilities.
  7. Confirm their ability to meet the W-9 and US bank account payment requirements.
  8. Submit before the September 13, 2026 deadline.

APPLY HERE

Why the Mycelia Fellowship Is an Important Opportunity

The Mycelia Fellowship stands out because it addresses a growing need for ethical approaches to storytelling.

In an era shaped by artificial intelligence, social media, digital surveillance, misinformation, and rapidly changing communication technologies, storytelling has become increasingly complex.

Stories can now travel globally within seconds.

However, rapid distribution creates important challenges.

For example:

  • Narratives can be removed from their original context.
  • Community stories can be appropriated.
  • Algorithms can determine which voices receive visibility.
  • AI systems can generate narratives without meaningful accountability.
  • Viral content can spread misinformation.
  • Historical information can disappear from digital platforms.

The fellowship creates space for practitioners to investigate these challenges while continuing their own work.

Its interdisciplinary structure also creates opportunities for collaboration between people working across:

  • Arts
  • Humanities
  • Research
  • Civic engagement
  • Technology
  • Community organizing
  • Storytelling

Visit HERE to learn more about the Mycelia Fellowship 2026.

Conclusion

The Mycelia Fellowship 2026 represents a unique opportunity for practitioners working at the intersection of storytelling, arts, humanities, civic engagement, and technology to deepen and expand projects that are already making an impact.

With only two fellows selected, the inaugural cohort will be small and highly selective. Successful applicants will receive a $2,000 stipend, direct advisory support from the Social Resonance Lab team, opportunities for increased visibility, and platforms to share their knowledge through writing, podcast participation, workshops, and public dialogue.

The fellowship is particularly valuable for practitioners interested in examining how stories shape communities and how power influences who has the ability to create, control, distribute, and interpret narratives.

Whether working through art as a form of civic participation or critically examining the effects of artificial intelligence and digital systems on collective memory and narrative autonomy, fellows will have an opportunity to contribute to important conversations surrounding the future of ethical storytelling.

Eligible United States-based practitioners with existing projects in storytelling, arts, humanities, civic engagement, or critical technology work should consider applying before the September 13, 2026 deadline.
